name: San Miguel de Allende
tagline: A pink-stone colonial town with a neo-Gothic parish church, cobbled lanes, courtyard hotels, galleries and rooftop terraces, popular with artists and expats for decades.
highlight: The pink spires of the Parroquia at sunset, from a rooftop bar on the Jardín.
shortDescription: A UNESCO-listed highland town of baroque churches, bougainvillea and galleries, with a big expatriate community, excellent restaurants and hot springs nearby.
metaDescription: A San Miguel de Allende travel guide: the Parroquia and the Jardín, Atotonilco sanctuary, galleries and rooftop bars, hot springs, Cañada de la Virgen, restaurants, where to stay and a two-day plan.
nearestAirport: Del Bajío (BJX), about 1 hour 15 minutes; Querétaro (QRO) about 1 hour
knownFor: The Parroquia, galleries, rooftop bars, expat community, hot springs
goodFor: Relaxed sightseeing, art, restaurants, a romantic break

image.alt: The pink neo-Gothic facade of the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel in San Miguel de Allende

intro: San Miguel de Allende sits at 1,900 metres in the highlands of central Mexico, founded by the Spanish in 1542 and enriched by silver and the road that carried it. It was almost abandoned in the early 20th century, and that neglect preserved its colonial centre. In the 1930s American artists arrived, including Stirling Dickinson, who founded an art school, and the town has been a magnet for creative visitors and retirees ever since.

Its symbol is the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel, whose pink neo-Gothic spires were designed in the 1880s by a self-taught indigenous builder who reportedly used postcards of European cathedrals as a guide. Around it, the Jardín, the central square, hosts musicians, vendors and families every evening, and the surrounding streets are lined with pastel houses, arched doorways and hidden courtyards. UNESCO listed the centre, and the nearby Sanctuary of Atotonilco, in 2008.

It is polished and relatively expensive, with a large foreign community, and some visitors find it too gentrified. Others enjoy it for that reason: good restaurants, boutique hotels, galleries and rooftop bars, with hot springs, vineyards and hiking a few minutes away.

whyVisit.intro: San Miguel is an easy, beautiful town for a relaxed few days, and a comfortable introduction to colonial Mexico.

points.title: A perfectly preserved centre
points.text: Cobbled streets, ochre and pink façades and courtyards make a compact and photogenic centre.

points.title: Art and crafts
points.text: Galleries, artisan markets and the Fábrica La Aurora arts complex reflect the town's artistic tradition.

points.title: Food and drink
points.text: Some of the best restaurants outside Mexico City, and rooftop terraces with views.

points.title: Hot springs and countryside
points.text: Natural thermal pools, wineries and hills lie close to the town.

points.title: A base for the region
points.text: Guanajuato and Querétaro are both within a couple of hours.

attractionsIntro: The centre is compact, and the sights are all within walking distance.

attractions.name: The Parroquia and the Jardín
attractions.text: The town's main church and its central square, shaded by laurel trees and busy on weekends. The pink stone glows at sunset.
attractions.tip: Sit on a bench and watch the evening promenade.

attractions.name: The Bellas Artes Cultural Centre
attractions.text: A former convent with a courtyard, murals by David Alfaro Siqueiros and a rotating programme of exhibitions and concerts.

attractions.name: Fábrica La Aurora
attractions.text: A former textile factory turned into a complex of galleries, design shops and cafés.

attractions.name: Mercado de Artesanías
attractions.text: A large craft market with tin, glass, ceramics and textiles.

attractions.name: The Santuario de Atotonilco
attractions.text: An 18th-century sanctuary with vividly painted walls and ceilings, called the Sistine Chapel of Mexico, and a key site for pilgrims.

attractions.name: Cañada de la Virgen
attractions.text: A pre-Hispanic pyramid complex 30 minutes from town, with astronomical alignments.

attractions.name: The Mirador
attractions.text: A hilltop viewpoint with a panorama of the town and its spires.

thingsToDoIntro: San Miguel is for wandering, eating and unwinding.

thingsToDo.title: Watch the sunset from a rooftop
thingsToDo.text: Several rooftop bars overlook the Parroquia, with mezcal cocktails.
thingsToDo.tip: Arrive before sunset to get a table.

thingsToDo.title: Soak in hot springs
thingsToDo.text: Thermal pools at La Gruta, Escondido Place and Xote, a short drive outside town.

thingsToDo.title: Take a cooking class
thingsToDo.text: Learn to make salsas, tortillas and mole from local cooks.

thingsToDo.title: Visit galleries and studios
thingsToDo.text: Dozens of galleries show contemporary Mexican art.

thingsToDo.title: Go horse-riding or hiking
thingsToDo.text: Trails run through the hills and along the Cañada de la Virgen.

thingsToDo.title: Sample local wine
thingsToDo.text: Vineyards in the Guanajuato wine region offer tastings.

foodIntro: San Miguel's restaurants range from Mexican classics to international cuisine, and the town has a strong farm-to-table scene.

foods.name: Modern Mexican
foods.text: Chefs reinterpret regional dishes with local ingredients.

foods.name: Tacos and street food
foods.text: Carnitas, al pastor and birria at stalls and taquerías.

foods.name: Guanajuato wine
foods.text: Reds and whites from nearby vineyards.

foods.name: Coffee and pastries
foods.text: Excellent cafés serve local coffee and baked goods.

accommodation.intro: Boutique hotels in restored mansions dominate, with a range of prices.

areas.name: Centro
areas.text: Boutique hotels and guesthouses within a few blocks of the Jardín.

areas.name: Guadiana and Ojo de Agua
areas.text: Residential neighbourhoods with guesthouses, a 15-minute walk from the centre.

gettingThere.intro: San Miguel is about 3.5 hours from Mexico City by road.

options.text: About 4 hours from the Terminal Norte.

options.mode: Flight to Del Bajío or Querétaro
options.text: Then a transfer of 1 to 1 hour 15 minutes.
About 1 hour 30 minutes by bus or car.

gettingAround.intro: The centre is small and walkable.

options.text: Sights are within 15 minutes of each other, on cobbled, sloping streets.
For hot springs, wineries and Atotonilco.

bestTime.headline: October–April
bestTime.summary: The climate is mild at 1,900 m, with a rainy season from June to September.

seasons.text: Dry, sunny and cool in the evenings.
Afternoon rain, green hills and lower prices.
Clear and pleasant, with Día de Muertos.

bestTime.avoid: Semana Santa and Christmas for crowds.

itinerary.title: Two days in San Miguel de Allende
itinerary.intro: The centre on the first day, hot springs and the sanctuary on the second.

days.title: The centre
days.morning: The Parroquia, the Jardín and the Bellas Artes centre.

tipsIntro: San Miguel is easy, and a few tips help.
tips: Wear flat shoes for the cobbles.
Visit the Jardín on a Sunday evening.
Prices are higher than elsewhere in Mexico.
Bring a jacket for the evenings.

faq.q: Is San Miguel de Allende worth visiting?
faq.a: Yes, for its architecture, food and atmosphere. It is touristy and expensive but very pretty.

faq.q: How many days do you need?
faq.a: Two or three, longer if you want to relax.
The town centre is generally safe, and popular with expats. Check your government's advice for Guanajuato state.

faq.q: How far is it from Mexico City?
faq.a: About 280 km, or 3.5 to 4 hours by road.
A pilgrimage sanctuary with painted walls, a UNESCO-listed site, near San Miguel.

faq.q: What is the best time to visit?
faq.a: October to April for dry weather.
